name: Od
catalog_citation: Grainger, Peter J. & Nita C. Grainger. 1980 (August). A preliminary survey of the languages of Sind, Pakistan. [Hyderabad, Sindh]: Language Project, Karachi Diocese (Church of Pakistan). 77 pp. + data appendix (140-page scan uploaded to archive.org by the Forum for Language Initiatives).
catalog_locator: printed p. 48 (PDF p. 53), Part III, section H.3 'The Phonological system of the languages', sub-heading 'Suprasegmental features'; Odki speaker/wordlist details pp. 30-31, lexicostatistic conclusions on Od p. 42, recommendation of further work on Odki p. 48.
catalog_quote: Suprasegmental features. None of the languages has phonemic word or syllable-tone so pitch has not been marked on individual words. With longer utterances, only Section H has some intonation recorded. [...] We found great difficulty in defining word-stress and it has not, therefore, been recorded. We suspect it is non-phonemic (i.e. predictable) in most of the languages. See Khubchandani (1962) for the rules with which stress can be predicted in Sindhi. A similar system works for Urdu and possibly the other languages in this survey.

Verification was done instead from the page renders of that PDF already sitting in the reader work dir (work_2026-09-20/disc/oddd1238/ = printed p. 48, = printed p. 44), which I viewed: p. 44 carries the heading '3 - The Phonological system of the languages' (pooled over all surveyed langua…
new_statements.relation_note: Consonant and vowel inventories pooled over all languages (Charts 3-4, pp. 46-47: implosives present in all tribal languages incl. Odki, vowel length hard to mark, nasalisation), then the suprasegmental paragraph quoted above.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For all surveyed Sind languages including the three Odki wordlist varieties: no phonemic (lexical) tone at word or syllable level; word stress was not transcribed because the surveyors could not define it consistently, and they suspect it is non-phonemic, i.e. predictable (by a Sindhi/Urdu-type rule, cf. Khubchandani 1962), 'in most of the languages' -- no placement rule is given for Odki itself.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the authors hedge ('we suspect', 'most of the languages', 'possibly the other languages in this survey')
new_statements.identity_note: The survey's languages 15-17 are 'Odki (Dadu)', 'Odki (Shikarpur)' and 'Odki (Pithoro)', wordlists taken from Od-caste speakers in upper and lower Sindh (pp. 30-31: Pastor David Ranjha of Dadu; Chatan Das, Shikarpur; Jetu s/o Damu of Pithoro, family formerly of Marwar) -- exactly the Dadu/Shikarpur/Pithoro Odki of Ethnologue/Glottolog odk/oddd1238 (this report is the source of those dialect names). The suprasegmental statement is a blanket one over all ~20 surveyed varieties (Sindhi, Siraiki, Dhatki, Marwari, Gujarati, the Koli languages, Odki, Bagri, Vaghri, Sansi, Urdu), not an Odki-specific paragraph.

sources.citation: Bughio, Abdul Basit & Abdul Malik Abbasi. 2026. A Metalinguistic Judgmental Analysis of Pakistani English Phonology by Odki Native Speakers. Linguistic Exploration 3(1): 103-114. DOI 10.55121/le.v3i1.1109 (CC-BY 4.0).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: An L2-English perception study of six Odki-L1 undergraduates in Karachi; contains no description or data of Odki itself and cites no Odki source. Only unsourced typological asides: p.107 'South Asian languages, such as Odki, are mostly syllable-timed, i.e., syllables are equally timed and accented'; p.110 'Because the participants' native L1 (Odki) is syllable-timed and lacks the complex "jumping" stress of English, the learners adopt a simplified rule: when in doubt, stress the end.' Not a statement of where Odki word stress falls.

sources.citation: David, Aneel (prepared by); checked with Gulzar Oad & Suhino Oad. [2011]. Word List in English, Urdu, Sindhi, Oadki & Oadki (IPA). [Hyderabad, Sindh]: Oadki Language & Community Development Organization (OLCDO). 11 pp. (Swadesh 207-item list plus additions, 245 entries, with an IPA column and gender/number suffixes).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No prose at all; broad IPA transcriptions (implosives, retroflexes, nasal vowels, occasional length mark) with NO stress or tone marks -- wordlist-only data, not a statement. Useful as the only IPA-transcribed Oadki lexical set and as evidence that an SIL-style orthography/phonology effort (Aneel David) existed c. 2011.

sources.citation: Institute of Applied Linguistics (IAL Trust, Karachi). n.d. [c. 2011-2020]. 'Grammar Feature List' -- Oadki entry (grammatical feature summary, pronoun chart, case markers, noun morphology chart), with companion 'Swadesh Word List' Oadki / Oadki (IPA) and (empty) 'Alphabet List' Odki. Online comparative database of the languages of Pakistan compiled by IAL staff and students.
sources.note: Nothing: Oadki is recorded with 2 genders, 4 cases, 3 tenses, gender-and-number agreement, ergativity 'yes', inclusive/exclusive 'we', near/far 3rd-person forms, dative نُون, genitive چا / چي / چِيان~چِيا / چين, noun class endings. The Swadesh Oadki (IPA) table reproduces the OLCDO 2011 transcriptions with no stress marks; the Odki alphabet table is empty. Shows IAL holds first-hand Oadki data (and lists, but does not post, 'Linguistic Working Papers Produced by IAL Students' for Oadki) -- the likeliest home of an unpublished Oadki phonology write-up.

The book is a narrative ethnography (a 'true story' of two friends plus Od customs, photos); the Odki material is a two-column Odki-Sindhi word list in Sindhi script (e.g. منک = ماڻهو 'man', استري = مائي 'woman') with no transcription, vowel marking or accent marks and no introductory note on pronunciation; p. 243 immediately before it is story text. The reference list (p. 247) adds two Sindhi-language pointers on the Ods not in our bibliography: Jial Odh 1993 on Od funeral customs and social life, and Dr Gulab Rai [Od], 'Dravidian - the historical background of the Od tribe', Sindhi…
